summary: A misconception-driven session correcting a sign error in eliminating simultaneous equations, building toward a reliable add-or-subtract rule.
student_turns: I've been doing simultaneous equations and I get properly confused about whether you're supposed to add them or subtract them.
So I've got 5x - y = 13 and x + y = 11. I subtracted them because that's what we did last time, and I got 4x - 2y = 2 and then I got stuck.
Wait, is it because the y's are +y and -y — different signs — so I should've added instead?
Okay so if I add them I get 6x = 24, so x = 4. How do I get y from there?
So y = 7 because 4 + y = 11? Can you give me a similar one so I know I've actually got it, not just memorised this question?

summary: A discouraged student who guesses at circle theorems at random, working toward checking each theorem's conditions before applying it.
student_turns: I keep messing up circle theorem questions and I don't know why, I just feel like I don't get any of them.
It's normally the ones where you have to work out which theorem to even use, not the actual working out bit.
I just kind of guess half the time. Like if there's a triangle in a circle I'll assume it's 90 degrees because of the angle in a semicircle one, even when it's not actually got the diameter in it.
How do I actually work out which theorem applies though? I never know where to start when I look at the diagram.
Okay so I could check first whether the triangle actually has the diameter as one of its sides before I assume it's a right angle?

summary: An exam-preparation session building toward choosing confidently between the sine rule, cosine rule, and area formula in non-right-angled triangles.
student_turns: I've got my maths mock next week and I really want to get better at knowing whether to use the sine rule or the cosine rule.
I think you use the sine rule when you've got an angle and the side opposite it, and the cosine rule when you haven't got a matching pair like that?
So if I'm given all three sides and I need to find an angle, that's the cosine rule rearranged to find the angle?
What about the area of a triangle — is that a totally separate formula, or does it use the same information as the sine rule?
Can you give me a mixed one where I actually have to figure out which rule to use myself, like it might come up in the exam?
